source_title: No winners if things go too far, Putin warns Europe amid Nordic outreach
source_excerpt:
Russian President Vladimir Putin warned that escalating tensions with Europe would leave no winners, while saying Moscow was open to restoring ties. His remarks followed a rare call with the leaders of Norway and Finland, who urged him to end the Ukraine war ahead of US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi.
Russian President Vladimir Putin said the leaders of Norway and Finland had made it clear during their phone calls with him that they did not represent the European Union, as he voiced support for restoring ties with European countries.
Putin said Russia was prepared for a potential war with Europe but did not want one, warning that “if things go too far, there will be no winners,” international news agency Reuters reported.
He also said Moscow did not want a situation similar to the one in the Strait of Hormuz to unfold in the Baltic Sea.
Putin's remarks come after Finnish President Alexander Stubb and Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store held a rare 90-minute telephone conversation with the Russian President on Tuesday, urging him to end the war in Ukraine and take part in meaningful negotiations for a stable and peaceful settlement. The call came ahead of planned United States-brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi early next month.
The outreach marked a departure from the longstanding reluctance among Western European leaders to engage directly with Putin. It also came as Brussels prepared for possible face-to-face discussions between European and Russian officials, although Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen criticised the Nordic initiative and said it had not been coordinated, German outlet Deutsche Welle reported.
Stubb described the exchange as candid and substantial. He said Finland and Norway shared borders with Russia and that the outcome of the war would directly affect their security as well as that of Europe. Direct dialogue, he added, was necessary to bring the conflict to an end.
Store highlighted the immense human and material cost of the war, saying its suffering and destruction would affect generations. He said the two leaders had emphasised the need for de-escalation during their conversation with Putin.
Finland and Norway are among Ukraine's biggest providers of military assistance. Stubb and Store informed Putin that this support would continue without interruption. The leaders also discussed security in the Baltic Sea region and the High North.
According to the Kremlin, Putin told the Nordic leaders that a fair and lasting peace could be achieved only if what he described as Russia's legitimate interests were considered fully and unconditionally. The formulation indicated that Moscow continued to press broad demands.
Stubb and Store initiated the call and later spoke with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy said the two leaders had conveyed to Putin that concrete de-escalatory measures were required concerning Ukraine's energy facilities and infrastructure. He thanked them for their active diplomatic backing and said Russia must stop prolonging the conflict.
The conversation was presented as a follow-up to the latest round of peace discussions in Oslo, jointly organised by Stubb and Store. Senior representatives from Ukraine, the US, the UK, Germany, Italy, the European Commission and NATO attended that meeting.
Russia did not participate in the Oslo discussions. However, US special envoy Steve Witkoff later travelled to St Petersburg to brief Putin about their outcome.
Another round of negotiations is expected in Abu Dhabi early next month. The proposed format will be similar to that used in Oslo, but a Russian delegation is expected to participate.
Brussels has said it is prepared for European and Russian officials to meet across the table, an arrangement that has not previously taken place during these negotiations. The European Commission and the European Council are working to form a joint team that would present the European Union's position. Both institutions are believed to have received advance notice of the Stubb-Store conversation with Putin.
The Finnish and Norwegian leaders stressed that they were not acting as special representatives for Europe, an issue that has divided European countries for more than a year. Frederiksen's swift criticism of the outreach reflected an uncommon disagreement among Nordic leaders.
The call reopened direct contact between the Nordic leaders and Moscow as diplomatic preparations continued for the Abu Dhabi talks. Stubb and Store pressed Putin to de-escalate and negotiate while reaffirming continued military support for Ukraine, even as questions remained within Europe over the coordination of such engagement. - Ends
